title: Where does God live?
hookLine: the Kotzker Rebbe answers his students: wherever people let God in (Hasidic tale)
tomorrow: the north wind and the sun

cards: Kids ask the best questions. Where was I before I was born? Why is the sky that color?
And, sooner or later: if God is real, where does God live? Adults tend to answer fast, and a little embarrassed: everywhere, sweetie.
Menachem Mendel of Kotzk, known as the Kotzker Rebbe, wasn't satisfied with the fast answer. He was a Hasidic master in Poland, remembered as fierce, brilliant and allergic to anything fake.
One day, the tale goes, he turns to a room of learned visitors and asks them that exact question: where does God live?

teach.h: THE WHOLE EARTH IS FULL OF HIS GLORY.
teach.b: The visitors laugh. What a question, Rebbe! Everyone knows the answer.
The prophet Isaiah says it. In his vision, the seraphim call out, in the King James words: "the whole earth is full of his glory." God is everywhere.
And the Kotzker shakes his head. No, he says.
God lives wherever people let God in. One small sentence, and the whole picture changes. The visitors' answer is true in their tradition: God fills the world.

But the rebbe is asking something else. Not where God is in theory, but where God is actually at home: where a presence is welcomed, noticed, given room. A house can be full of air and still feel shut.
The Hebrew tradition has a word for God's indwelling presence, Shekhinah, from a root that means to dwell, to live somewhere.
The Kotzker's point is that the dwelling isn't only up to God. It's also a door that people open, or keep closed.

For listeners who don't use the word God, the story still speaks: whatever you call what's sacred, awe, love, presence, it tends to live where it's let in. Now look back at this week. zil g'mor. haruv. Zusya's question.
Two pockets. The whistle. The treasure under the stove.

And now, where does God live. Seven tales from Jewish tradition, and nearly every one turns on something small and close: one line, one tree, one self, one note, one whistle, one stove, one open door.

how: The Kotzker's saying is quoted in Jewish teaching and sermons, and Jewish homes traditionally have a mezuzah on the doorposts, which some people touch on the way in and out as a reminder of God's presence.

games.q: you're one of the learned visitors. the Kotzker Rebbe asks: where does God live? what do you say?
o: everywhere: the whole earth is full of his glory.
games.why: the visitors give the textbook answer, and laugh. the rebbe says: God lives wherever people let God in.

practice: If you can, go to a door, any door, open it, and stand in the doorway; if you can't move right now, picture one. Feel the air change, and the threshold under your feet.
If you pray, let God in, in your own way; if you don't, let in whatever is sacred to you: stillness, gratitude, the day itself.

wordCard.voice: Shekhinah, God's indwelling presence. The Kotzker Rebbe's answer to where God lives: wherever people let God in.

carryVoice: Your line: let it in. The door is yours to open. That closes the Jewish wisdom week, day sixty-three.
